events.title: NFS released
events.summary: Sun Microsystems shipped the first Network File System in August 1984 — remote file access over TCP/IP that made networked disks look local.
events.about: NFS let workstations mount directories from a server as if they were local drives — bootless Sun workstations, shared home directories, and centralized `/usr` trees. Built on ONC RPC and XDR, it became the default way Unix machines shared files before SMB dominated Windows shops. Every `mount server:/export/home` traces back to Bill Joy's team at Sun.

narrative.whyChosen: NFS was the first widely deployed network filesystem for Unix workstations.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved transparent remote file access could work at LAN scale and influenced later distributed storage designs.
narrative.problemSolved: Diskless workstations and multi-user labs needed shared files without copying data to every machine.

sources.title: Sandberg et al. — The Sun Network Filesystem (USENIX 1985; implementation began March 1984)

events.title: IBM PC AT released
events.summary: IBM announced the Personal Computer AT in August 1984 — a 6 MHz 80286 machine with 16-bit ISA slots and a 20 MB hard drive.
events.about: The AT introduced the 80286 CPU and 16-bit expansion bus to the IBM PC line — OS/2 and early Windows protected-mode software targeted this hardware. Clone makers shipped AT-compatible machines that extended the PC standard. The model name "AT" (Advanced Technology) set expectations for each generation of PC upgrades through the 1990s.

narrative.whyChosen: The PC AT brought 16-bit computing and the 80286 to the mainstream IBM-compatible market.
narrative.whyImportant: It extended the open PC architecture that software and hardware vendors built on for decades.
narrative.problemSolved: The original PC and XT were hitting limits on speed and memory for business applications.
